demo:
def greet(name):
    print("Hello,", name)

# "Perth" is the argument
greet("Perth")
note: The value is the argument; the name it arrives under inside the function is the [[parameter]].
short: The actual value you hand to a function when you call it.

demo:
def area(width, height):
    # width and height are the parameters
    return width * height

print(area(3, 4))
note: A parameter is a name waiting for a value; an [[argument]] is the value that turns up.
short: The name a function gives to a value it is handed, written in its def line.

demo:
def double(n):
    return n * 2

result = double(21)
print(result)
print(double(5) + 1)
note: Returning is not printing. A function that prints shows you something; a function that returns gives you something you can use.
short: Hands a value back to whoever called the function, and stops the function there.

demo:
def shows(n):
    print(n * 2)

value = shows(21)
print("the call was worth:", value)
note: A function that prints instead of returning gives the caller nothing: the call is worth None.
short: Writes something on the screen for a person to read.

demo:
def nothing():
    pass

print(nothing())
print(None is None)
note: A function with no return statement hands back None, which is why printing its result shows None.
short: Python's word for "no value at all".

demo:
prices = [3, 5]
prices.append(7)
print(prices)
note: Changing a mutable value changes it for every name pointing at it — see [[aliasing]].
short: Able to be changed after it is made. Lists, dictionaries and sets are mutable.

demo:
name = "perth"
upper = name.upper()
print(name)
print(upper)
note: Operations that look like changes build a new value instead and leave the old one alone.
short: Cannot be changed once made. Strings, numbers and tuples are immutable.

demo:
a = [1, 2]
b = a
b.append(3)
print(a)
print(a is b)
note: Assigning a list to a second name does not copy it. Use list(...) or a slice to get a copy.
short: Two names pointing at the same value, so a change through one shows through the other.

demo:
days = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"]
print(days[0])
print(days[-1])
print(len(days))
note: The last item is at index len(x) - 1, which is why len(x) itself is out of range.
short: The position of an item in a list or string, counting from 0.

demo:
word = "Fremantle"
print(word[0:4])
print(word[:3])
print(word[-3:])
note: The stop position is not included, so x[0:2] gives two items.
short: A piece of a list or string, written x[start:stop].

demo:
point = (3, 4)
x, y = point
print(x, y)
print(len(point))
note: Like a list but immutable, which makes it safe to use as a dictionary key.
short: A fixed sequence of values, written with round brackets: (1, 2).

note: Asking for a key that is not there raises KeyError; .get() returns None instead.
short: The thing you look something up by in a dictionary.

note: Looping over a dictionary gives you its keys, not its values.
short: To go through something one item at a time, which is what a for loop does.

demo:
total = 0
for n in [2, 4, 6]:
    total = total + n
print(total)
note: It has to be created before the loop starts, or the first pass has nothing to add to.
short: A variable you set up before a loop and add to inside it.

demo:
print(2 + 2)
print("ab" * 3)
print(5 > 3)
short: A piece of code that produces a value: 2 + 2, name.upper(), x > 3.

note: An expression produces a value; a statement does something.
short: A complete instruction: an assignment, an if, a loop, a return.

demo:
print(3 > 5)
print(bool(0), bool(""), bool([]))
print(bool("no"), bool([0]))
note: Python also treats 0, "" and [] as false when it needs a yes or no, which is what "falsy" means.
short: A value that is either True or False.

demo:
print(0.1 + 0.2)
print(7 / 2)
print(round(2.675, 2))
note: Floats are stored in binary, so some sums come out a hair off: 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3.
short: A number with a decimal point, like 3.5.

demo:
print(7 / 2)
print(7 // 2)
print(-7 // 2)
note: Dividing with / always gives a float; // keeps it whole and rounds down.
short: A whole number, with no decimal point.

demo:
first = "Swan"
print(first + " River")
print(first + str(2))
note: Both sides have to be strings: adding a number raises TypeError unless you convert it first.
short: To join two strings end to end with +.

demo:
name = "  perth  "
print(name.strip().title())
print("a,b".split(","))
note: A method acts on the thing before the dot, which is why it needs no argument for it.
short: A function that belongs to a value, called with a dot: name.upper().
A named block of code you can run whenever you want, by calling it.

demo:
def f():
    inside = 1
    print("inside sees:", inside)

f()
print("outside sees:", "inside" in dir())
note: That is why a variable made in a function vanishes when the function ends.
short: Where a name can be seen. A name made inside a function is only visible inside it.

note: Read it from the bottom: the last line names the error, and the line above it is usually your code.
short: The report Python prints when something goes wrong, listing where it happened.

note: try/except lets you catch one and decide what to do instead of stopping.
short: Python's way of stopping when it cannot carry on, like dividing by zero.

note: A SyntaxError means Python could not read the code at all, so nothing ran — not even the lines above it.
short: The grammar of the language: where the colons, brackets and indents go.

note: Four spaces per level is the convention. Mixing tabs and spaces is a common cause of errors.
short: The spaces at the start of a line, which is how Python knows what is inside what.

note: Without one the calls never stop, and Python gives up with RecursionError.
short: The case a recursive function answers directly, without calling itself again.

note: Every recursive function needs a [[base-case]] or it never stops.
short: A function that calls itself on a smaller version of the same problem.

note: A project brief that fixes a signature means calling it that exact way, with that many parameters.
short: The def line of a function: its name and the parameters it takes.
A value written directly in the code: 42, "hello", [1, 2].
A value an operator works on. In 2 + 3, the operands are 2 and 3.

note: A nested loop runs its whole inner loop for every single pass of the outer one.
short: One thing inside another: a loop inside a loop, or a list inside a list.

note: Everything else prices off it: a forward is spot plus the cost of waiting, a differential is a premium or discount to it.
short: The price for a cargo delivered now, rather than on some date in the future.

note: A barrel is not a barrel. Two cargoes at the same volume can be worth several dollars apart because of what comes out of them at the refinery.
short: A named type of crude oil with its own chemistry and its own price, such as Brent, WTI or Dubai.

note: Light and sweet is the easy stuff; heavy and sour needs a more expensive refinery, which is why it trades at a discount.
short: How light or heavy a crude is. Higher API means lighter, and lighter usually means more petrol and diesel per barrel.

note: Sulphur has to be taken out before the fuel can be sold, so sour crude sells at a discount to sweet — the discount is roughly what removing it costs.
short: Crude with a lot of sulphur in it. Low sulphur is called sweet.

note: Physical oil is almost never quoted as a flat price. It is quoted as the benchmark plus or minus a differential, and the differential is where a physical trader actually competes.
short: The premium or discount a particular cargo trades at against its benchmark grade.

note: Crude usually moves in cargoes of 500,000 to 2 million barrels, which is why physical trading is a business of few, large, slow decisions.
short: One shipload of a commodity, bought and sold as a single unit.

note: Its shape is an instruction: upward ([[contango]]) pays you to store, downward ([[backwardation]]) pays you to sell now.
short: The prices quoted today for delivery in each future month, drawn as a line across those months.

note: The shape that fills tanks — but only where it is steeper than the [[carry]].
short: A forward curve that rises with time: oil for later delivery costs more than oil now.

note: The market saying it wants the barrel today. It empties storage, because holding stock means selling it forward for less than you paid.
short: A forward curve that falls with time: oil now costs more than oil later.

note: The number a contango has to beat. On an $80 barrel at 5%, six months of financing alone is $2.
short: Everything it costs to hold a barrel until a later date: tank rent, insurance, and interest on the money tied up in it.

note: A storage trade is a bought time spread with a tank behind it: you own the near month and are short the far one.
short: The price difference between the same commodity for two different delivery months.

note: It is the toll on every location trade, and it moves on its own: a route can stop working because ships got expensive, with no change in the oil price at all.
short: What it costs to move a cargo from one port to another, usually quoted per barrel or per tonne.

note: The arb is open when that gap is wider than the [[freight]] between them, and closed when it is not. Traders say "the arb is shut" to mean the cargo stays home.
short: The price difference for the same commodity in two places.

note: The standard unit of long-haul crude. When the curve is steep enough, traders hire them to sit still as floating storage.
short: A very large crude carrier: a tanker holding about two million barrels.

note: Miss one limit by a fraction and the cargo is off-spec, which can turn a premium product into a discounted one instantly.
short: The quality a buyer has contracted for: limits on sulphur, density, flash point and the rest.

note: The classic asset-backed margin: buy the cheap off-spec barrel, blend it against something better, sell the mixture at the on-spec price.
short: Mixing two or more parcels so the result meets a specification neither of them met alone.

note: A refinery is long the crack whether it likes it or not, which is why refiners hedge by selling it.
short: The gap between what a refinery pays for crude and what it gets for the fuels it makes from it.

note: Hedge a sour cargo in Nigeria with Brent futures and you have swapped price risk for the risk that the two stop moving together. That gap is where hedged traders still lose money.
short: The risk left over when what you hedged with is not exactly what you own.

note: The cruelty of hedging physical: the paper leg demands cash today while the barrels it protects pay nothing until they are delivered.
short: A demand for more cash from the exchange when the market moves against your futures position.

note: It is why a perfectly hedged trader can still run out of money: the hedge is settled daily, the cargo is settled once.
short: Settling a futures position's gain or loss every day, in cash, rather than at the end.
